site.title: Self & Other
site.tagline: An illustrated guide to the immune system and the new science of cancer immunotherapy
site.shareImageAlt: Self & Other: glowing immune cells under the microscope. An illustrated guide to the immune system and cancer immunotherapy.

parts.title: The Immune System
parts.subtitle: The cells and molecules of immunity, and how they distinguish the body’s own cells from everything else

parts.title: Cancer and the Immune System
parts.subtitle: What cancer is, why it is hard for the immune system to detect, and how tumors escape

parts.title: Immunotherapy
parts.subtitle: What each kind of treatment does, whom it helps, what it costs and where it falls short

pages.label: Chapter 1
pages.title: Cells, Proteins and Molecular Recognition
pages.description: Cells, genes, proteins and molecular binding: the basic biology behind every act of immune recognition.

pages.label: Chapter 2
pages.title: Innate Immunity
pages.description: Within minutes of a splinter, your body mounts a defense against bacteria it has never encountered and never needs to identify.

pages.label: Chapter 3
pages.title: Adaptive Immunity
pages.description: The body makes millions of random receptors in advance, then multiplies the cells whose receptors bind a new pathogen.

pages.label: Chapter 4
pages.title: Antigen Presentation
pages.description: Nearly every cell displays samples of the proteins it makes inside, which is how T cells tell healthy cells from infected or mutated ones.

pages.label: Chapter 5
pages.title: T Cells: Selection, Killing and Regulation
pages.description: How the body builds T cells that can recognize almost anything, and keeps them from attacking its own tissues.

pages.label: Chapter 6
pages.title: Cancer Cells and Tumor Antigens
pages.description: Cancer is evolution within one body. Its cells are almost entirely self, so the immune system must detect the few things about them that are new.

pages.label: Chapter 7
pages.title: Immune Surveillance and Tumor Escape
pages.description: The tumors that reach a doctor are the ones that survived the immune system, and they carry the marks of that selection.

pages.label: Interlude
pages.title: 130 Years of Immunotherapy
pages.description: A century of inconsistent results, from Coley’s bacterial toxins onward, then rapid progress after 2010.

pages.label: Chapter 8
pages.title: Checkpoint Inhibitors
pages.description: Checkpoint inhibitors do not attack cancer cells; they release brakes on T cells. For a minority of patients, the benefit lasts for years.

pages.label: Chapter 9
pages.title: Therapeutic Antibodies
pages.description: An antibody can only bind. Medicine has turned that one property into five ways to treat cancer.

pages.label: Chapter 10
pages.title: Cell Therapies
pages.description: Medicines that are cells rather than molecules: they multiply inside the patient, kill on contact, and can still be present a decade later.

pages.label: Chapter 11
pages.title: Cancer Vaccines and Oncolytic Viruses
pages.description: The most successful cancer vaccines never show the immune system a cancer cell. The newest are made from the mutations in one patient’s tumor.

pages.label: Chapter 12
pages.title: Resistance and New Directions
pages.description: Why immunotherapy cures some people and does nothing for others, and what researchers are trying next.
